question: Which of the following is SHARED among all threads within the same process?
options: Heap memory and open file descriptors
Stack memory and registers
Thread local storage and program counter
Process ID (PID) and call stack frames
correct_answer: Heap memory and open file descriptors
explanation: Threads share process address space including code, data, heap, and open OS resources. Each thread maintains its own unique call stack and CPU register state.

question: To prevent a deadlock from occurring, which of the following is sufficient according to the Coffman conditions?
options: Eliminate at least ONE of the four Coffman conditions.
Eliminate ALL four Coffman conditions simultaneously.
Ensure CPU utilization remains below 80%.
Assign every process an equal scheduling priority.
correct_answer: Eliminate at least ONE of the four Coffman conditions.
explanation: All four Coffman conditions must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to exist. Breaking any single condition guarantees deadlock prevention.

question: In a virtual memory system with paging, what happens when a page fault occurs?
options: The referenced page is loaded from secondary storage into physical RAM
The operating system terminates the process immediately
The CPU switches to hyperthreading mode
A context switch to another core is forced
correct_answer: The referenced page is loaded from secondary storage into physical RAM
explanation: A page fault is an interrupt raised by the memory management unit (MMU) when a program accesses a valid virtual page that is not currently resident in physical RAM. The OS loads the required page from disk.

question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm can lead to starvation for processes with long burst times?
options: Shortest Job First (SJF)
Round Robin (RR)
First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
Lottery Scheduling
explanation: Shortest Job First (SJF) always gives precedence to processes with the shortest remaining burst time. If short processes arrive continuously, longer processes may wait indefinitely (starvation).

question: What is the primary purpose of a mutual exclusion lock (mutex)?
options: Preventing more than one thread from executing in a critical section concurrently
Allowing multiple threads to read and write shared data without synchronization
Speeding up CPU instruction caching across cores
Preventing page replacement in virtual memory
correct_answer: Preventing more than one thread from executing in a critical section concurrently
explanation: A mutex guarantees mutual exclusion: only one thread can acquire the lock and execute the protected critical section at any given time, preventing data races.

question: Why is a thread context switch within the same process generally faster than a full process context switch?
options: Threads share the same virtual memory space, so page tables and TLB entries do not need to be flushed
Threads do not require saving CPU registers
Thread switching is handled exclusively by hardware without OS intervention
Threads have no execution stack
correct_answer: Threads share the same virtual memory space, so page tables and TLB entries do not need to be flushed
explanation: Because threads within the same process share identical virtual memory mappings (page tables), a thread switch avoids invalidating the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), greatly reducing memory cache misses.
